question: Had the bike for a year, put about 15 hours on it ... I am bottoming out on the face when I seat bounce them. Yet on square edge bumps the bike is harsh feeling. ... Do I need to add more HSC in the shock to help?
message_sent: Had the bike for a year, put about 15 hours on it ... I am bottoming out on the face when I seat bounce them. Yet on square edge bumps the bike is harsh feeling. ... Do I need to add more HSC in the shock to help?
rider_context: 6'4", 180-185 lb before gear; ~15 hours; upgraded to firmer rear spring and set sag; low-speed compression adjuster maxed out; rear fender buzz from tire; fork pressure changes made little difference

response.summary: Don’t add shock high-speed compression first: it may reduce bottoming but worsen the square-edge harshness. Check the shock spring and sag, then try slightly firmer low-speed compression for jump-face support.
response.answer:
**Not as the first move.** More HSC can resist bottoming, but it can also make those square edges harsher. Seat-bouncing loads the shock heavily; harshness plus bottoming can mean it’s riding too deep, not simply that compression is too firm.

At your **203 lb geared weight**, KTM specifies a **shock spring 45 N/mm** for the 187–209 lb band. Check the fitted spring, then set **105 mm rider sag** and check against **35 mm static sag**. Too little static sag with correct rider sag points to a spring that’s too soft—fix that before chasing clickers.

If spring and sag check out, common tuning practice is:
- **Shock low-speed compression: turn in 2 clicks from your current position** for more support on a smoothly loaded jump face; leave HSC unchanged initially. KTM’s stock references are **15 clicks out LSC** and **2 turns out HSC**, not assumed to be your current settings.

Compare a normal standing approach with your seat-bounce on a familiar jump you already ride consistently; avoid an abrupt seated hit into the face.

Your 15 added hours aren’t necessarily total shock hours. KTM calls for its first shock service at **20 hours**, then every **40 hours**; unknown previous service matters here.

question: I'm really struggling with the "twitchy" front end feel on my 2023 250. The front end feels so twitchy and has a tendency to tuck on corner entry or speed wobble on decel. ... Will 24mm OS triple clamps help?
message_sent: I'm really struggling with the "twitchy" front end feel on my 2023 250. The front end feels so twitchy and has a tendency to tuck on corner entry or speed wobble on decel. ... Will 24mm OS triple clamps help?
rider_context: ~150 lb, intermediate (stated in a later reply); already had suspension revalved by local tech, tried forks flush in the clamps, tried adding more sag; stock springs

response.summary: 24 mm-offset clamps may calm this generation’s front end, but check mechanical condition and braking balance before buying. More offset reduces trail, so the reported improvement is not simply extra straight-line stability.
response.answer:
**Yes—24 mm-offset clamps can help this generation, but they’re not a guaranteed cure for decel wobble or entry tuck.** Several testers and owners report improvement with 23–24 mm clamps; that’s experience, not Honda’s prescribed fix.

Importantly, going from the reported stock 22 mm to 24 mm offset reduces trail by about **2.2 mm**, worked out from the supplied geometry assuming everything else stays unchanged. It doesn’t add trail or automatically make the bike more stable.

Before spending money:
- Check steering-head and wheel-bearing play, tire condition/bead seating, spokes and fork alignment. Don’t tune around looseness or binding.
- Measure rider sag: Honda’s stock-spring target is **105 mm**. At your **170 lb geared**, keep the springs as the starting point and use rider/free sag and travel use to judge them—not weight alone.
- Separate the fork behavior: diving before the tuck points toward more compression support; staying high and deflecting points toward less. Getting lower through successive braking bumps points toward faster rebound.

**My pick: sort those checks first; if the twitchiness remains, 24 mm clamps are a reasonable next purchase**, with fitment verified for your 2023 CRF250R. Stop riding if the wobble becomes violent or anything is loose.

question: I should have .44 fork springs and a 4.3 kg shock spring at 140 pounds with no gear. ... the preload collar is all the way loose and I'm only getting 91mm of race sag. Any ideas why I'm not able to get the correct sag?
message_sent: I should have .44 fork springs and a 4.3 kg shock spring at 140 pounds with no gear. ... the preload collar is all the way loose and I'm only getting 91mm of race sag. Any ideas why I'm not able to get the correct sag?
rider_context: C-class MX rider, 140 lb without gear; installed .44 fork springs and 4.3 kg shock spring from Race Tech calculator; greased linkage; measured sitting near the front; year not stated

response.summary: At 91 mm rider sag with the preload backed off, verify the measurement and free suspension movement before buying a softer spring. Your stock fork is air-sprung, and KTM’s shock-spring chart points to 42 N/mm for your saved 160 lb geared weight.
response.answer:
**91 mm is short of KTM’s 105 mm rider-sag target—but don’t loosen the collar farther if the spring is becoming loose.** The spring must remain seated with the rear wheel hanging.

First, a hardware correction: your stock WP XACT AER fork uses air, not .44 coil springs, unless it has been converted. If “4.3 kg” means 4.3 kg/mm, that’s approximately 42 N/mm—close to KTM’s **shock spring 42 N/mm for 143–165 lb riders**. Your 140 lb without gear and saved 160 lb geared weight don’t immediately suggest that rate is wrong.

Check these in order:
1. **Measurement:** measure axle-to-SAG-mark with the rear wheel hanging, then with you seated in full gear, feet on the pegs and a helper balancing the bike. Settle it several times. KTM’s targets are **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**.
2. **Binding:** compare where the rear settles after pushing it down versus lifting it and letting it settle. A noticeably different result points to friction in the linkage, swingarm or shock—not a clicker problem.
3. **Actual spring:** if measurements repeat and movement is free, verify the spring’s stamped rate and correct fit. A stiffer-than-assumed spring or remaining preload can explain insufficient sag.

**What static sag do you measure with nobody on the bike?**

question: i got yz250f 2024 and i am wondering if the stock shock and fork springs are proper for me. I am 158lbs without gear, c class mx rider. ... do you think stock valving will be okay for me or i will need revalve?
message_sent: i got yz250f 2024 and i am wondering if the stock shock and fork springs are proper for me. I am 158lbs without gear, c class mx rider. ... do you think stock valving will be okay for me or i will need revalve?
rider_context: 158 lb without gear, C-class MX; online spring calculators disagree; thinks 5.4 N/mm shock spring is fine

response.summary: Keep the stock springs and valving to start. At your weight and C-class motocross pace, a revalve is unlikely to be your first worthwhile expense.
response.answer:
**Yes—the stock springs are a sensible starting point for you, and I’d keep the stock valving.** At 158 lb without gear, with 178 lb geared saved, you’re not someone I’d automatically respring for C-class motocross.

Yamaha’s stock rates are **fork springs 4.7 N/mm** and **shock spring 56 N/mm**. That’s a starting recommendation, not a weight-chart guarantee: Yamaha doesn’t publish a rider-weight spring chart for this bike.

Confirm the shock spring by setting Yamaha’s **90–100 mm rider sag**, measured seated in full gear, then measuring free sag with you off the bike. Very little free sag at correct rider sag points to a spring too soft; excessive free sag points to one too stiff. Fork dive and bottoming during your normal riding help judge the fork springs.

For the valving, stock is the sensible common-practice choice at your pace. Testers consistently report that the 2024 fork can dive, but that alone doesn’t mean you need a revalve—get springs, sag and clickers right first. Spend on valving only if you can’t get both comfort and support.

response.summary: Don’t soften it further yet. At 195 lb geared, your softer springs, reduced oil and fully open compression could leave the fork riding too deep rather than make it more comfortable.

**I wouldn’t remove more oil or go softer on springs yet.** Testers consistently report harsh stock suspension on this RM-Z250, but you’ve already made substantial changes in that direction.

At your **195 lb geared**, the .46 fork springs deserve checking before chasing more damping changes. If you mean .46 kg/mm, they’re considerably softer than the consistently reported stock **fork spring 5.0 N/mm**. Softer springs plus 20 cc less oil and fully open compression can let the fork ride deep, where it can still feel harsh.

- If it dives and uses most of its travel, try fork compression **2 clicks in from fully open**, leaving everything else alone; compare over the same section.
- If it rides high and barely moves, check fork alignment and friction first. With compression already fully open, a revalve is more useful than further softening blindly.

The shock’s fully open high-speed compression can also let the rear ride low and upset front-to-rear balance. Measure rider and free sag before choosing a shock spring or changing preload.

question: my 2021 MC450 has 12 hours on it now. ... I've reduced air pressure down to 140, and reduced comp clickers, but the forks seem way stiff to me ... Should i go less than 140psi? how low is too low?
message_sent: my 2021 MC450 has 12 hours on it now. ... I've reduced air pressure down to 140, and reduced comp clickers, but the forks seem way stiff to me ... Should i go less than 140psi? how low is too low?
rider_context: 12 hours; rear spring changed 42 -> 45 N/mm; XACT air fork lowered to 140 psi with compression clickers reduced; still cannot bottom the fork; can bottom the rear with stock clickers

response.summary: Don’t drop below 140 psi blindly—too little air can make these forks feel harsher by riding too deep. Check compression direction, bleed trapped outer-chamber air, and address the first fork service due at 10 hours.
response.answer:
**I wouldn’t go below 140 psi yet.** GASGAS’s stock pressure is **10.7 bar (155 psi)**; you’re already 15 psi below that. Too little air lets the fork ride deep in its stroke, which can feel stiff rather than plush.

GASGAS lists an adjustment range of **7–12 bar (102–174 psi)**, in **0.2 bar (3 psi)** steps. That lower limit is not a recommended target: too low for you means excessive dive, low ride height or frequent bottoming.

Check what you mean by “reduced compression”: **fewer clicks out makes it firmer**. Standard is **12 clicks out**, comfort **17 clicks out**, counted from lightly seated. The compression adjuster is on top of the right leg.

Before another pressure change, with the forks cold and front wheel lifted, release trapped air through both outer-chamber bleeder screws, then close them again—don’t vent the main air-spring valve. Check main pressure cold in that same unloaded position.

Common tuning practice: if it barely uses travel and deflects, test 3 psi less; if it dives and rides deep, don’t lower it further. Change only one thing per test.

At **12 hours**, it’s also due for GASGAS’s first fork service: **once after 10 hours, then every 40 hours**.

question: the stiffness is getting to me when the track develops a lot of breaking/acceleration bumps ... if I decrease compression ... it tends to fold/dig/plow in the deep sand in the turns ... could leave me any tips or clicker settings/air pressure
message_sent: the stiffness is getting to me when the track develops a lot of breaking/acceleration bumps ... if I decrease compression ... it tends to fold/dig/plow in the deep sand in the turns ... could leave me any tips or clicker settings/air pressure
rider_context: Deep sand tracks; AER48 air fork at 162-164 psi, comp 13 out, reb 20 out, forks at second line; shock sag 98 mm, HSC 1.5 out, LSC 8 out, reb 16 out; letting air out makes the bike not stay on top of the dirt (post says 2021, thread title says '22)

response.summary: Put compression back where it was before softening it—the digging got worse because you lost front-end support. If harshness builds through successive bumps, try faster fork rebound instead.
response.answer:
Put the compression back where it was before you softened it. Your result suggests the fork needs that support in sand; opening compression further lets it ride deeper and dig rather than making it comfortably softer. Several testers found the same deep-riding, pitching tendency on this generation.

For your **2021 US 350 SX-F**, KTM’s stock baseline is:

| Setting | Standard |
|---|---:|
| Fork air, cold | 10.6 bar (154 psi) |
| Fork compression | 12 clicks out |
| Fork rebound | 18 clicks out |
| Shock low-speed compression / rebound | 15 / 15 clicks out |
| Shock high-speed compression | 2 turns out |
| Rider / static sag | 105 / 35 mm |

Try these separately:
- **Fork compression:** return to your pre-softening position to recover sand-turn support.
- **Fork rebound:** if the first bump feels okay but each following bump gets harsher, open it **2 clicks from where it is now** so it can recover. Undo that if the front becomes springy or climbs out of ruts.

Check air cold with the front wheel unloaded; bleed the outer chambers, not the main air spring. Don’t lower main pressure blindly—weight and travel use decide that.

In sand, use a round turn and steady light throttle; practise five controlled passes without chopping the throttle mid-turn.

question: advice on suspension setting going from MX to trail race ... Have a 2024 YZ450F on stock suspension ... Not looking to revalve or respring ... Looking for good advice on where to go from my base setup to give me the best shot at being comfortable

response.summary: Start by softening fork compression two clicks, then shock high-speed compression one-sixth turn. Keep enough support for race-speed hits rather than opening every adjuster.
response.answer:
Keep your stock springs and start with **small reductions in compression damping**, not everything wound soft. For a trail race, you want the wheels absorbing roots and edges without the bike diving or wallowing.

Record your MX settings first, bleed trapped fork air with the front wheel unloaded, and check sag in gear. Yamaha specifies **90–100 mm rider sag**; keep your existing measured balance initially rather than changing sag and damping together.

Try these individually:
1. **Fork compression: 2 clicks farther out than your MX setting** for less sting through the bars. Yamaha’s stock reference is 10 clicks out—not necessarily where yours is now.
2. **Shock high-speed compression: 1/6 turn farther out than your MX setting** for sharper roots and square edges. Yamaha’s stock reference is 1 turn out. Several testers found this shock firm on high-speed compression.
3. **Only if the fork resists small bumps or gets lower through repeated hits: fork rebound 2 clicks farther out.** Stock reference is 11 clicks out; faster recovery can help, but reverse it if the front becomes springy.

These follow Yamaha’s stock-suspension tuning directions. Test each over the same short loop; undo a change that adds bottoming, pitching or deflection. Clickers can improve comfort, but won’t make MX valving behave exactly like dedicated woods suspension.

What’s your weight in gear, current damping settings, and terrain—mostly roots/rocks or fast, flowing dirt?

Before changing anything, record your settings. Kawasaki’s stock fork baseline is **compression 14 clicks out, rebound 12 clicks out**, counted from lightly seated; that’s a reference, not confirmation of what’s currently fitted. Check rider and free sag before chasing clickers.

question: does anyone know the standard click settings for the suspension on an CRF 250R 2024. Just bought the bike and trying to work out the best settings. which settings do you suggest for a 170kg rider on sand, hard pack etc.

response.summary: Honda’s stock clicker settings are below, but at 170 kg (about 375 lb), springs matched to your weight come before sand or hard-pack clicker tuning.
response.answer:
**At 170 kg (about 375 lb), I’d sort the springs first—not try to hold the bike up with clickers.** Assuming the suspension is still stock, these are Honda’s standard settings:

| Adjuster | Standard position |
|---|---:|
| Fork compression—both legs | **12 clicks out** |
| Fork rebound—both legs | **13 clicks out** |
| Shock low-speed compression | **6 clicks out** |
| Shock high-speed compression | **2 1/6 turns out** |
| Shock rebound | **11 clicks out** |

Count out from gently seated clockwise; Honda counts the first click as position 1. Fewer clicks out means firmer damping. **Never exceed 16 clicks out on either fork adjuster.**

Honda lists fork springs **4.8 N/mm** and shock spring **50 N/mm** as standard; its optional stiff choices are fork springs **5.0 N/mm** and shock spring **52 N/mm**. As general tuning guidance, at your weight I’d expect even those optional springs to be insufficient. A suitable heavier spring package and matching valving are the priority; an exact rate needs sag measurements, not guesswork. Honda’s standard-spring rider-sag target is **105 mm**; don’t force that with excessive preload.

After the springs and balance are right, use these small, common-practice tests—not a complete setup for your weight:
- **Springs:** move to weight-matched fork and shock springs; confirm with rider sag, free sag and bottoming resistance.
- **Sand:** if starting at stock, fork compression **12 → 11 clicks out** for more support, following Honda’s sand-setting direction.
- **Hard pack:** separately, from stock, fork compression **12 → 13 clicks out** for grip and compliance, provided it isn’t diving or bottoming.

Test one change over the same section for a few laps. What rider sag and free sag do you measure now, with free sag measured bike-only on its wheels?

response.summary: The spiky feel does not prove the frame or subframe is moving uncontrolled. With broad rear adjustments failing to cure it, check mechanical freedom and chassis integrity before chasing more settings.
response.answer:
An uncontrolled frame or subframe wiggle is possible if something is loose or damaged, but **the spiky feel alone doesn’t establish that**. Some owners report the same sharp rear-chassis feel on the 2025, with suspension adjustments only partly helping; no single cure is established.

You’ve already swept sag from 107 to 102 mm and tried hard-to-soft damping. That makes another blind clicker sweep a poor next move. Honda’s standard-spring sag target is **100 mm**, but reaching that number won’t explain or cure binding or looseness.

I’d separate these possibilities:
- **Binding or play:** linkage, swingarm or steering bearings, fork alignment, or loose frame/subframe attachments can transmit sharp hits regardless of clicker position.
- **Suspension riding too deep:** a soft spring or slow rebound can feel hard; softer compression can actually worsen it.
- **Chassis feedback:** plausible after those checks, but not evidence of a defective frame.

First, with the engine off and bike securely supported, inspect frame/subframe joints for cracks or movement and check wheel, steering and linkage play and smoothness. **Don’t ride with cracks, loose attachments or detectable bearing play.**

There is also a reported handlebar-clamp recall affecting 2025–2026 models: have Honda check your VIN and remedy status before further testing.

response.summary: Remove the fork legs to reduce the outer-chamber oil accurately; don't try extracting it through the air-release screws. Removing 5 ml mainly softens the end of the stroke, not the initial harshness.

**I’d remove the fork legs—not try sucking oil through the air-release screws.** Those screws release trapped air; they aren’t a reliable way to remove a measured amount of outer-chamber oil. Common workshop practice is to remove the legs and drain/refill accurately.

Honda specifies **5 cm³ (5 ml) steps per leg**. With the standard fork springs, the outer-chamber baseline is **380 cm³ per leg**, so one step down is **375 cm³**, provided they actually contain the standard volume now. Honda’s permitted range is **323–410 cm³ per leg**.

Less oil softens the fork **near full compression**. It won’t do much for a stiff first part of the travel, and can increase bottoming. Test the same section afterward; restore the previous volume if bottoming increases without improving comfort.

At 73 kg—about 161 lb—you’re in the lighter group that testers consistently found these forks harsh for. Honda offers an optional **fork spring 4.6 N/mm**, versus the standard **fork spring 4.8 N/mm**; that’s the softer direction to assess if the fork barely moves, rather than repeatedly lowering oil.

question: just picked up my first ever KX and want to check/set sag. I'm 185lbs dry, slow vet, for mx only. The ring nuts aren't easily accessible especially with spanners. Anyone familiar with the KX rear shock provide some advice or tips in getting to and adjusting the rings?

response.summary: The KX250X preload rings are awkward to reach; the reviewed access procedure removes the rear frame and airbox. Measure sag first so you know whether adjustment is needed.
response.answer:
**Measure sag before fighting the rings.** On your 2021 KX250X, the reviewed access procedure removes the rear frame and airbox to give the hook wrenches room—not a hammer-and-punch adjustment through the gap.

1. Measure rear axle to a marked point on the rear fender with the rear wheel fully extended. Repeat with you standing on the pegs in full gear, then with just the bike on its wheels. Subtract each from the extended measurement for rider sag and free sag; settle the suspension before each reading.
2. **Start around 105 mm rider sag** for MX—common tuner practice, not a Kawasaki-published target. Roughly 30–40 mm free sag is a general cross-check. Your 185 lb dry weight and saved 205 lb geared weight make checking spring suitability worthwhile; very little free sag at correct rider sag points to a spring that's too soft.
3. For proper ring access, the job removes the seat, side covers, tank, muffler and battery, then disconnects the rear-frame wiring and intake duct before removing the rear frame/airbox. Cover the exposed intake.
4. With the rear wheel unloaded, loosen the upper locknut using hook wrenches. Move the adjusting nut **down the shock for more preload/less sag**, or up for less preload/more sag. Work in small increments, lock the rings together and remeasure after reassembly.

Kawasaki's standard preload-nut position is **123.1 mm**, measured from the upper shock-pivot center; the permitted range with the standard **shock spring 54 N/mm** is **120.6–132.6 mm**. That is a nut-position measurement, not sag. Rear-frame bolts tighten to **35 Nm (26 ft-lb)**; reconnect everything and remove the intake cloth before starting. Never ride with the locknut loose.

question: I just picked up a 2020 fc250 ... I am 185 pounds ... as i have been getting faster my suspension has just gotten worse ... i also dont know how to set sag on my own. What would you guys recommend
message_sent: I just picked up a 2020 fc250 ... I am 185 pounds ... as i have been getting faster my suspension has just gotten worse ... i also dont know how to set sag on my own. What would you guys recommend
rider_context: 185 lb (180-190); fast beginner, ~2 years riding MX tracks in Texas; stock air fork; adjusts clickers and air pressure without a method; cannot set sag; quoted $1,500 for revalve + spring conversion

response.summary: Start with sag and a known stock baseline—not a revalve. At 185 lb geared, you’re near the top of Husqvarna’s standard rider-weight band; sag will tell us whether the shock spring works for you.
response.answer:
**Set sag and establish a baseline before buying suspension parts.** Getting faster puts more load into the suspension, but “worse” could mean bottoming, harshness or kicking—and those need different fixes.

At your saved **185 lb geared**, Husqvarna’s 165–187 lb band calls for a **shock spring 42 N/mm**. Confirm what spring is fitted; don’t assume a used bike still has stock suspension. If it’s revalved, get the tuner’s baseline for your weight instead.

### Measure sag
You’ll want a lift stand, tape measure and a helper. Holding the bike upright and measuring accurately by yourself is difficult.

1. Rear wheel hanging free: measure rear axle to the fender’s SAG mark. Call this **A**.
2. Bike upright on its wheels, nobody aboard: measure again, **B**. **A − B = static sag; target 35 mm (1.38 in).**
3. Wearing your gear, sit normally with feet on the pegs, bounce and settle. Have your helper measure **C**. **A − C = rider sag; target 105 mm (4.13 in).**

Less spring preload increases rider sag; more preload reduces it. If rider sag is correct but static sag is well below target, the spring is too soft; well above target points to too stiff. This bike’s reviewed preload-adjustment procedure requires shock removal—don’t hammer the collar around.

### Baseline to check
Record every current setting first, then check these Husqvarna stock values:
- **Sag:** establish 105 mm rider / 35 mm static before tuning damping.
- **Shock:** low-speed compression 15 clicks out; high-speed compression 1.5 turns out; rebound 15 clicks out.
- **Fork:** air 10.4 bar (151 psi), fully extended and cool; compression and rebound each 12 clicks out.

Count out from lightly seated—never force an adjuster. Inspect for leaks or binding before tuning, then test one change at a time on the same section.

Tap **“Start a guided job”** above the message box and choose **“Set the suspension back to the standard baseline and check the sag.”** Have a fork pump and screwdriver ready too.

What does “worse” feel like most: bottoming, harshness through the bars, or the rear kicking?

**Changes to try, one at a time:**
- **Rear sag:** Measure current sag against 105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag before adjusting damping.
- **Shock baseline:** After recording current positions, check stock low-speed compression at 15 clicks out, high-speed compression at 1.5 turns out, and rebound at 15 clicks out.
- **Fork baseline:** After recording current settings, check stock air pressure at 10.4 bar (151 psi), compression at 12 clicks out and rebound at 12 clicks out.

response.summary: Start from KTM’s 15-click-out shock rebound baseline, but identify how the rear kicks before choosing faster or slower rebound.
response.answer:
**Kicking doesn’t always mean the shock rebound is too fast—slowing it can make repeated-bump kicking worse.** Suspension tuners commonly find three different causes.

For the stock 2024 250 SX, KTM’s shock rebound baseline is **15 clicks out**, counted counterclockwise from lightly seated. Record the existing position before resetting it.

Then test one change at a time:
- **Straight-up kick after one hit or a jump face:** from the 15-out baseline, try **13 clicks out** to slow the return.
- **First bump feels fine, then the rear gets lower and harsher:** try **17 clicks out** instead, allowing it to recover between bumps.
- **Sideways deflection off sharp edges:** compression is the stronger suspect; don’t automatically slow rebound. KTM’s standard shock high-speed compression is **1.5 turns out**.

Before testing, check for leaks, linkage play and an overly tight chain. KTM’s sag targets are **105 mm riding / 35 mm static**; incorrect spring support or rear ride height can cause kicking that rebound won’t fix. For revalved suspension, use the tuner’s baseline instead.

message_sent: I'll be picking up a '24 Yz 250x at the dealer tomorrow. I live in Northern Arizona at 5,700ft and most of my riding will be between that and 8,000ft. ... I am looking to see if anyone has any jetting info for high elevations.

response.summary: Your 5,700–8,000 ft riding will generally need leaner jetting than the stock baseline. Have the dealer confirm what is installed before changing anything; the exact altitude-specific combination isn't confirmed here.
response.answer:
Yes—at **5,700–8,000 ft**, your YZ250X will generally want **leaner jetting than its stock baseline**, especially in warm weather. Ask the dealer to record what jets and needle position they deliver it with rather than assuming it's untouched.

Yamaha's stock US settings are:
- Main **#178**, pilot **#52**, power jet **#55**.
- **NYHW needle, clip in groove 2**.
- Air screw **1-1/8 turns out**, although Yamaha individually sets it at the factory—record its actual position first.

The exact altitude-specific combination isn't confirmed here. **Common tuning practice:** if it blubbers at large throttle openings once warm, try the next smaller main-jet step first and retest. If it's rich through the middle afterward, raising the needle clip one groove lowers the needle and leans that range. Change only one item at a time; don't automatically lean every circuit together.

An engineering estimate at 5,700 ft and 60°F, assuming 50% humidity, puts air density around **81% of standard**—enough to explain why sea-level jetting can feel loaded up. That does not translate directly into a jet-size percentage.

**Stop if it pings or detonates.** What temperatures will you usually ride in?

I’d check these in order:

2. **Pressure-sensor flange and signal:** GasGas specifically calls for inspecting that flange for cracks and damage. Check its sealing, connector and live signal before condemning the sensor.
3. **Fuel delivery and ignition:** Have the dealer correlate sensor readings, fuel pressure, injector leakage and ignition performance with the fouling. A reflash cannot fix a leaking injector, false sensor input or weak spark. Exact pressure and sensor test limits aren’t confirmed here.

Verify the fuel is mixed at GasGas’s **1:60** ratio. At 24 hours, also confirm the **15-hour minor engine service**, including piston replacement and exhaust-control checks, was completed; that isn’t proof the piston caused this.

response.summary: Daily plug fouling needs sorting, but gentle riding could explain it. A suitable hotter plug and properly clearing the engine under load are the common first fix—not a guaranteed cure for this fuel-injected 125.
response.answer:
**Yes—if it’s loading up from gentle riding, the common first fix is a suitable one-heat-range-hotter plug and getting it properly warm under load.** That helps burn deposits off; it isn’t a reason to push the kid beyond his comfort level or rev it endlessly on the stand.

The exact hotter replacement isn’t confirmed for this bike, so have KTM confirm a compatible option before fitting one. KTM specifies **NGK BR10 ECMVX**, **0.80 mm (0.0315 in)** gap and **25 Nm (18.4 ft-lb)** tightening torque for the standard plug.

I’d tackle it in this order:
1. Check the failed plug: dry black soot supports low-temperature fouling; wet fuel can also mean flooding or weak ignition.
2. Use fresh fuel with KTM’s specified **1:40 premix** and the correct two-stroke oil—don’t change the oil ratio to cure fouling. Avoid prolonged idling; have a capable rider give it a clean run under load, then see whether it survives the next normal ride.
3. If it still fouls daily, check filter condition, plug-cap/coil connections and idle speed (**1,400–1,500 rpm**), then have fuel pressure and injector sealing tested. It’s EFI: no jets to change.

question: Just installed my twinair powerflow kit to my 24 kx450. ... The bike "bogs" a bit when twisting the throttle hard ... Are any of you guys running my setup and could share some mapping tips? Maybe give it some more fuel, but where and how much?

response.summary: Check the PowerFlow installation before adding fuel. If the bog happens under load, a small low-rpm fuel increase is a reasonable test, but there is no confirmed PowerFlow-specific map here.
response.answer:
**Check the PowerFlow fit first—don’t assume the bog means it needs more fuel.** Since you’ve just fitted it, check the filter-to-cage seal, cage seating, intake boot and whether excess filter oil is restricting airflow.

For mapping, Kawasaki’s **RIDEOLOGY THE APP KX** edits fuel and ignition on a **6 × 6 rpm/throttle grid**, separately for Full and Mild modes. Save your existing map before changing anything; make app changes only while stopped.

The exact PowerFlow-specific fuel correction isn’t confirmed for your bike. **General tuning practice:** if installation checks pass and it hesitates while accelerating under load, try the smallest positive fuel increment the app permits in the low-rpm cells covering the throttle opening where it hesitates. Leave ignition and higher-rpm cells alone initially. Repeat the same controlled roll-on; keep the change only if response clearly improves, and revert if it becomes blubbery or worse. Don’t richen the whole grid.

**Does it bog while riding under load, or only when snapping the throttle open on the stand?** That distinction matters before choosing cells. Stop testing if it knocks, repeatedly stalls or develops a fuel leak.

**Go one size down—from the #50 pilot to a #48 first.** Several owners report cleaner bottom-end running with a leaner pilot, and #48 is a tuner-tested starting point—not Yamaha’s factory setting.

Keep your 110/93 fuel blend and 32:1 mix unchanged during that test so you’re changing only one thing. Yamaha specifies 30:1 with Yamalube 2R; don’t change premix ratio to cure rich jetting.

Record your air-screw position first. Yamaha’s standard is **1¼ turns out**; out leans the low-speed mixture, in richens it. With the engine warm, compare small-throttle response on the same section: you want less blubbering and clean pickup without a hanging idle or surging. Don’t jump to #45 unless the #48 still proves rich after air-screw adjustment.

If it stays excessively rich, check the filter for excess oil and the carburetor for overflow or a float-valve problem rather than continuing to fit smaller pilots. **Stop if it pings or detonates.**

question: If I ride my 125 at a track and love the jetting, but it's 70-80f outside ... temps could be 38-50f now during the winter ... Is there a generic starting point where you'd go, "1 larger main jet" or "drop the clip 1 line."
message_sent: If I ride my 125 at a track and love the jetting, but it's 70-80f outside ... temps could be 38-50f now during the winter ... Is there a generic starting point where you'd go, "1 larger main jet" or "drop the clip 1 line."
rider_context: Carbureted 125 two-stroke (make/year not given); jetting is good at 70-80F, now riding at 38-50F

response.summary: Yes—one main-jet size richer is a common first test for that temperature drop. Change the needle clip only if the midrange also needs richer jetting.
response.answer:
**Yes—start one main-jet size richer than your good 70–80°F setup**, as general tuning practice, not a guaranteed winter setting. Assuming the same elevation, fuel and premix, riding at 38–50°F means denser air, which makes your existing jetting run leaner.

1. **Main jet: go one available size larger than your warm-weather main.** This addresses roughly ¾ to full throttle. Confirm the main before changing the needle; one size may not be enough at the cold end of your range.
2. **Needle: leave the clip alone initially.** If it then feels lean specifically at ¼–¾ throttle, lower the clip one groove from its warm-weather position. That raises the needle and richens the midrange.

Test one change at a time with the engine warmed up and progressively applied load—not a long wide-open pull straight away. Clean, consistent pull without lean surging is the goal; blubbering suggests too rich. **Stop immediately if it pings or detonates.**

question: 2023 250x. Fresh complete rebuild ... after 3-8 seconds it dips down way too low and it dies. The idle hangs regardless of jetting, needle position, air screw adjustment, or idle speed screw adjustment. ... Any suggestions at all would be appreciated
message_sent: 2023 250x. Fresh complete rebuild ... after 3-8 seconds it dips down way too low and it dies. The idle hangs regardless of jetting, needle position, air screw adjustment, or idle speed screw adjustment. ... Any suggestions at all would be appreciated
rider_context: Fresh top/bottom rebuild (stock bore, OEM piston); V-Force 4 reeds, Apex XC head, FMF Gnarly/Shorty; power jet plugged, TPS deleted; 91 octane with Klotz premix; tried timing changes; leak-down holds 8.5 psi; fresh gas/plug, clean filter; throttle cable and power valve OK

response.summary: Stop chasing jetting for now. A hanging idle followed by stalling immediately after a complete rebuild puts an intake/crankcase air leak or a carburetor installation fault ahead of another jet change.
response.answer:
**Check for an air leak before running it again.** Since jets, needle position, air screw and idle screw changes haven’t cured it, another jetting change isn’t the next move.

My order of suspicion:
1. **Unmetered air after the rebuild:** intake boot/reed-block sealing, cylinder base gasket, crank seals or crankcase sealing. Extra air can hold the revs up, then leave it too lean to keep running.
2. **Slide or cable not closing:** with the engine off, confirm the slide closes positively and doesn’t lift when you turn the bars. Yamaha specifies throttle-grip free play of **3.0–5.0 mm (0.12–0.20 in)**.
3. **Pilot circuit or bowl-supply trouble:** a blocked pilot passage, incorrect float setting or restricted fuel supply can cause a brief run followed by stalling. Yamaha’s stock float height is **6.5 mm (0.26 in)**, checked by the correct measurement procedure—not guessed from fuel level.

The decisive next test is a **two-stroke crankcase pressure-and-vacuum leak test**, including the intake sealing. Use a proper regulated tester; never connect shop air directly. If you don’t have that equipment, have the rebuilder perform it before break-in. Don’t spray flammable cleaner around a running engine to hunt the leak.

question: I have a 2023 KTM 300 SX. Last time out with 2.6 hours on the bike the bike just shut off for a second. ... it did it again! ... My KTM dealer ... said they couldn't duplicate the problem ... Any suggestions?

response.summary: An intermittent shutoff is not normal, even if the dealer couldn’t reproduce it. Start with an engine-off vent and wiring inspection, then have the dealer check stored faults and fuel delivery during the failure.
response.answer:
**Don’t dismiss it as break-in.** A dealer finding nothing while it runs normally doesn’t rule out an intermittent fault.

A few owners of the 2023 TBI 250/300 SX report similar brief cut-outs, with the throttle-position-sensor wiring, fuel pickup/filter and tank vent suspected—but no confirmed common fix.

I’d check these in order:
1. **Engine off and fully cool:** inspect the tank vent hose for pinching, especially around the steering head. Don’t ride with the cap loose to test it.
2. Inspect the accessible TPS connector/pigtail, plug cap, battery connections and grounds for looseness, moisture, chafing or heat damage. Don’t adjust the TPS or replace it on suspicion alone.
3. Ask the dealer to read stored fault memory and investigate fuel pressure and electrical supply **during the complaint**, rather than just checking that it starts. KTM specifies an initial fault-memory read and fuel-pressure check after 1 operating hour. The exact fuel-pressure acceptance figure isn’t confirmed here; the dealer needs KTM’s test procedure.

**Avoid jumps and racing until this is resolved:** another cut-out could happen on a jump face.

response.summary: That isn’t normal. Check the idle setting first: Husqvarna specifies 1,500–1,700 rpm; if it won’t hold that, investigate the plug, intake and EFI rather than carburetor jetting.
response.answer:
First check the idle setting—**Husqvarna specifies 1,500–1,700 rpm** for your 2023 TC 250. Running properly with the throttle open but dying as it closes points first toward insufficient idle opening, though it doesn’t prove that’s the fault.

Your bike is **fuel injected**: there’s no pilot jet or carb air screw to change.

1. With the engine off, confirm the throttle snaps fully closed. Then, outdoors with the bike secure and in neutral, check the warm idle with a tachometer and use the designated idle adjuster—not throttle-cable tension—to set it within that range.
2. If it still won’t idle, inspect the air-filter seating, intake boot and ignition connectors. Husqvarna lists intake leaks and loose or oxidized ignition connections among causes of stalling.
3. Check the plug for wet fouling: the specified plug is **NGK BR 8 ES**, gap **0.60 mm (0.0236 in)**. If the malfunction lamp is lit or flashing, have the EFI fault memory read before buying parts.

Don’t ride it until it reliably returns to idle; stop testing if it races or the throttle sticks.

Did this start suddenly after previously idling normally, or has it done this since you got it?

response.answer:
**I’d put the backfire screen back in.** Removing it may reduce intake restriction slightly, but there’s no confirmed performance gain for your 2021 CRF450R here—especially something you could reliably judge after only 15 minutes.

As general EFI guidance, the ECU compensates for air temperature and atmospheric pressure; that isn’t the same as measuring every bit of extra airflow from an intake modification and automatically adding the right fuel. The screen also helps protect the foam filter from an intake backfire. For now, refit it, keep the filter properly oiled and seated, and evaluate the bike in Standard mode while you get familiar with it. If you later change the intake and exhaust, use a matching tune verified under load rather than assuming it needs more fuel.

**Separate check:** Honda recalled certain 2021 CRF450Rs for a drive chain that could break. Have a Honda dealer check whether yours needs the free chain replacement or has already had it.

response.summary: Yamaha’s 2022 stock baseline is a #160 main, #75 pilot and NYDF needle in clip 2—not the GYTR setup. A severe bog needs checking before assuming it needs larger jets.
response.answer:
For your **2022 YZ125**, Yamaha’s stock jetting is below—but it is **not a GYTR baseline**. Don’t mix individual stock settings into the GYTR combination blindly.

| Setting | Yamaha stock baseline |
|---|---|
| Main jet | **#160** |
| Pilot jet | **#75** |
| Needle | **NYDF, clip 2 from top** |
| Power jet | **#35** |
| Pilot air screw | **2-5/8 turns out nominal**; individually factory-set |

Yamaha’s general-terrain examples specify:
- **59–77°F:** the baseline above.
- **Above 77°F:** #162 main, #72 pilot, NYEF clip 2, #35 power jet; air screw **1/4 turn farther out than its factory setting**.
- **Below 50°F:** #162 main, #75 pilot, NYDF clip 2, #35 power jet; factory air-screw position.

Owners commonly describe the GYTR kit as a **Y4 needle and #70 power jet**, with the pilot purchased separately; reported results vary. Other owners have experienced lean-feeling bogs with aftermarket combinations, but a bog alone doesn’t establish lean jetting.

What main/pilot/power jets, needle/clip and air-screw position are actually fitted, at what throttle opening does it bog, and what town/elevation and temperature are you riding in?

Separately, US 2022 YZ125s had a gear-shift assembly recall. Have Yamaha check whether yours needs the free repair; stop riding if it shifts unexpectedly or won’t select gears.

response.summary: Traction-control intervention is the first possibility to separate from a misfire: unloading the rear wheel at a lip can trigger power reduction. Restarting clears the symptom, but does not prove the cause.
response.answer:
This could be **traction control cutting power as the rear wheel unloads**, rather than an engine failure—but popping with lost drive needs checking before you jump again.

Your 2025 CRF250R has Honda Selectable Torque Control. Honda says it watches how quickly engine rpm rises, then retards ignition and controls fuel injection to reduce power; it does not need wheel-speed sensors. A throttle blip as the rear wheel leaves a lip could trigger it. That fits the timing, but does not prove the popping is normal. The selected traction-control setting stays saved, so restarting is not simply switching it off.

If it also happens with the rear tire firmly hooked up, intermittent ignition, wiring or fuel delivery becomes more likely. Don’t change fueling maps to cover it up.

**First, record the selected traction-control level and any warning-light pattern**, without trying to reproduce it on a jump. If a warning appears, capture it before switching off, provided it is safe to do so.

Does it happen only as the rear wheel unloads at the lip, or also accelerating on ordinary ground?

Separately, have Honda check whether the April 2026 handlebar-clamp recall applies and whether the repair is complete.

question: I have a 2020 Kawasaki KX250 that is seemingly leaking oil from the valve cover ... the bike has only 18 hours on it, and it seems to only happen when it starts to get hot out. ... could the bike just be getting too hot?
message_sent: I have a 2020 Kawasaki KX250 that is seemingly leaking oil from the valve cover ... the bike has only 18 hours on it, and it seems to only happen when it starts to get hot out. ... could the bike just be getting too hot?
rider_context: 18 hours; valve cover/seal recall already done by dealer; Tusk 1.8 radiator cap gauge read ~350 (red zone); oil and filter changed every 5-7.5 hours, air filter nearly every ride

response.summary: Hot weather can expose a weak valve-cover seal, but an oil leak alone does not prove overheating. Find the first wet spot before replacing parts or tightening bolts.
response.answer:
**It could be running hot, but a valve-cover oil leak by itself doesn’t prove overheating—and isn’t normal at 18 hours.** Hot oil flows more easily, so a marginal seal may only leak once the engine warms up.

Most likely, in order:
1. **Valve-cover gasket or bolt sealing washers:** a damaged, displaced or poorly seated seal can seep when hot. Oil from higher up can also track along the cover seam.
2. **Restricted crankcase breather or excess oil:** either can encourage oil out through a weak seal.
3. **Actual overheating:** more likely if there’s also steam, coolant loss or boil-over—not simply warmer weather.

With the engine off and fully cold, clean and dry the cover area, then inspect the gasket seam, bolt washers and accessible breather hose for damage or pinching. Check oil level by Kawasaki’s inspection-window procedure; don’t judge it from the amount poured in alone.

**Don’t crank the cover bolts tighter to stop it:** Kawasaki specifies **10 N·m (89 in-lb; 7.4 ft-lb)**. A damaged seal needs resealing, not extra torque.

Don’t ride until the source is identified; oil reaching the exhaust, falling oil level, steam or coolant loss means stop and repair it. Never remove a hot radiator cap.

Where does the oil first appear: the cover seam, around a cover bolt, or above the cover?

question: my friend just bought a New Gas Gas MC 350 ... minimal smoke at idle ... as soon as he turns the throttle, wow cloud of blue smoke. ... do these bikes come with engine oil in the crate, or does the dealer put the engine oil in?

response.summary: A cloud of blue smoke when the throttle opens is not normal new-bike break-in. Check the oil level without running it again, then have the selling dealer verify the delivery preparation.
response.answer:
Gas four-stroke dirt bikes commonly arrive factory-filled, with the dealer checking the oil during delivery preparation—but the exact shipping-fill arrangement for this MC 350F isn't confirmed here. The dealer should verify what was already in it before adding any.

**A big blue cloud under throttle is not normal break-in.** It likely means oil is burning; don't keep revving it to “clear it out.” Check these possibilities in order:
- **Overfilled oil:** excess oil can carry through the crankcase breather into the intake.
- **Oil in the intake from transport or tipping:** inspect the breather and airbox for pooled oil.
- **Internal oil-control trouble:** rings, cylinder or valve seals need checking if the level and intake are correct.

With the engine cold, hold the bike upright on level ground: GasGas specifies oil at the **middle of the sight glass**. If already warm, wait **1 minute after shutdown**; the level should be between the middle and top edge. Don't restart it just to warm it. The oil-change fill is **1.0 l (1.1 US qt)**—not an amount to add blindly.

Have the selling dealer document and correct the smoking before riding.

Separately, US recall CPSC 25-283 names 2023–2025 GasGas MC models for possible front-caliper failure. Have the dealer confirm applicability and whether the repair is complete; affected bikes must not be ridden until remedied.

question: I was riding at a sand track and all of sudden ... I suddenly felt a significant increase in vibration in my hands and feet. ... My bike has 44 hours on it. ... possibly a bearing has gone out in the oil pump?
message_sent: I was riding at a sand track and all of sudden ... I suddenly felt a significant increase in vibration in my hands and feet. ... My bike has 44 hours on it. ... possibly a bearing has gone out in the oil pump?
rider_context: 2020.5 model; 44 hours; keeps air filter clean, oil changed every 5-7 hours; buddy heard possible knocking at idle

response.summary: A sudden, significant vibration increase is not normal—stop riding until the cause is identified. An oil-pump fault is possible, but loose mounts, drivetrain trouble and internal engine faults need separating first.
response.answer:
**Stop riding and don’t restart it just to reproduce the vibration.** A sudden increase through both the bars and pegs at 44 hours deserves checking; hours alone don’t identify a failed bearing.

My check order would be:
1. **Engine mounts, head braces and exhaust mounts:** something loosening or contacting the frame can suddenly transmit much more engine vibration.
2. **Chain, sprockets and wheels:** damaged teeth, a tight chain section, packed sand or a wheel/tire problem can cause vibration tied to road speed rather than engine rpm.
3. **Internal engine or lubrication trouble:** a balancing-system, crank bearing or oil-pump-drive fault becomes more concerning if there was new noise, power loss or metal in the oil.

KTM specifies two trochoidal oil pumps. That does **not** establish that an oil-pump bearing has failed; pump drive, condition and oil pressure need checking before replacing parts. The exact oil-pressure test specification isn’t confirmed here; KTM’s engine repair manual carries it.

First, with the engine off and cool, inspect the mounts, exhaust and accessible drivetrain for looseness, damage or contact marks. Don’t ride with anything loose, an oil leak or unexplained mechanical noise.

**From what you already noticed, did the vibration follow engine rpm or bike speed?**

**Don’t run extra engine oil—it won’t fix this, and overfilling can cause other problems.** Keep it at the correct level using the bike’s specified checking method.

Boiling over within five minutes on the stand can come from lack of airflow through the radiators; a motocross bike shouldn’t sit idling that long. That alone doesn’t prove an engine fault.

Check these in order:
1. **Let it cool completely**, then check coolant level, external leaks, and mud or bent fins blocking the radiators. Never open the cap hot.
2. Inspect the radiator-cap seals and filler neck. A cap that won’t hold pressure lets coolant boil sooner; have the cap and cooling system pressure-tested if coolant loss repeats.
3. If it also overheats while moving, investigate circulation/water-pump trouble, then combustion leakage into the cooling system. Immediate pressure buildup from cold or repeated coolant expulsion makes combustion leakage more suspicious.

Don’t keep restarting it to reproduce the boil-over, and don’t ride with low coolant or repeated overheating.

question: Just got the kid a new 22' KTM 125 SX. ... noticed it was leaking oil where the pipe connect to the head. ... dealer ... said it was normal and needed to be broken in. ... Is this normal? Will it cause harm to the bike?

response.summary: A little oily exhaust residue is common on a two-stroke, but a leaking pipe joint should not be dismissed as break-in. Minor seepage usually will not hurt the engine; check the pipe seal and mounting.
response.answer:
**A little black, oily residue is common on a two-stroke—but break-in is not a repair for a leaking pipe joint.** That pipe connects to the cylinder, not the cylinder head.

The residue is usually unburned premix oil mixed with exhaust deposits, often called spooge. Gentle riding and a cool exhaust can produce more of it. A small smear normally will not damage the engine, but repeated dripping, exhaust puffing or a loose pipe points to a sealing or fitment problem.

With the engine and pipe cold, clean the joint and inspect the pipe seating, retaining springs and mounts. If the residue returns, have the dealer check the joint’s sealing rings and pipe alignment rather than simply waiting for break-in. Don’t tighten the mounts harder to force it to seal.

KTM specifies **1:40 premix** for this bike; don’t reduce the oil to hide the leak or push the kid to ride harder to clear it.

question: I just picked up a 22 tc 250. Has 4.2 hours on it. ... I go to ride it and it has no power ... maybe the power valve isn't opening at all? Or maybe the clutch is dragging?
message_sent: I just picked up a 22 tc 250. Has 4.2 hours on it. ... I go to ride it and it has no power ... maybe the power valve isn't opening at all? Or maybe the clutch is dragging?
rider_context: 4.2 hours; bought used; previous owner installed full Rekluse auto clutch and FMF pipe and silencer; little power except right off the bottom; intermittent knock

response.summary: A power valve that stays closed could explain weak upper-rpm power. Clutch drag usually causes creeping or stalling—not an engine that simply won't make power.
response.answer:
**The power valve is possible, but clutch drag isn't the usual cause of “no power.”** First separate an engine that won't pull from a clutch that won't transmit the pull.

- **Power valve staying closed:** it may run reasonably down low, then feel flat as the revs climb instead of pulling harder. Don't turn the preload adjuster to troubleshoot an unverified fault.
- **Clutch slipping:** the engine revs rise, but speed doesn't follow, with rear-wheel spin ruled out. **Clutch drag** instead makes it creep with the lever pulled in, hard to select neutral, or stall when selecting gear.
- **Fueling/intake trouble:** bogging, blubbering or refusing to rev points here before the clutch. A choke left on, restricted filter or stale fuel can do it—even with only **4.2 hours**, especially after storage.

Start with the engine off and cold: check that the choke is fully off, the filter is properly seated and unobstructed, and the throttle moves freely and snaps shut. Don't run it with a sticking throttle; stop for metallic knocking, pinging, fuel leakage or overheating.

**When you say no power, does it rev cleanly without accelerating, or does the engine itself bog and refuse to rev?**

response.answer:
**Yes—budget for a full top-end inspection, but don’t order only a piston kit yet.** If that 80% leakdown is valid, sealing is seriously compromised; sand on the piston raises concern for abrasive wear to the cylinder, rings and valve seats. The reported 34 hours doesn’t rule that out.

Before dismantling, verify the leakdown at compression TDC with both valves closed and the crank safely restrained:
- Air at the intake points toward intake-valve leakage.
- Air at the exhaust points toward exhaust-valve leakage.
- Heavy leakage into the crankcase points toward rings, piston or cylinder damage.

Incorrect crank position, decompressor action or a leaking tester connection can distort the result. Have a shop repeat it if you cannot safely restrain the crank.

Then inspect the piston/rings, measure the cylinder and check its coating, and assess valve faces/seats. Trace the sand through the filter seal, cage, airbox and intake boot before rebuilding. Check the drained oil and filter for grit or metal; bottom-end work depends on contamination and bearing condition, not leakdown alone.

You said **2019**, while the selected bike is a 2020. Exact 2019 clearance and wear limits aren’t confirmed here; use the 2019 Suzuki service manual’s valve-clearance and cylinder/piston sections. I wouldn’t judge your .006/.002 readings without confirmed units.

**Do not start it or try to run the sand through.**

question: Currently on a 21 Gas Gas 450 which I use for motocross ... Bike has 125 hours on it. I did a top end/ timing chain at 95. ... Is it reasonable to expect the engine to be trouble free at 120-200 hours?
message_sent: Currently on a 21 Gas Gas 450 which I use for motocross ... Bike has 125 hours on it. I did a top end/ timing chain at 95. ... Is it reasonable to expect the engine to be trouble free at 120-200 hours?
rider_context: 125 hours, mostly MX practice; top end and timing chain at 95 hours; valves in spec; oil every 4 hours; does not over-rev

response.summary: Reaching 200 hours is possible, but expecting trouble-free motocross use without further engine work is not a sound plan. The top end at 95 hours did not reset the bottom end’s service life.
response.answer:
**Possible to reach 200 hours, yes; reasonable to count on trouble-free running, no.** At 125 hours, your piston and timing chain have 30 hours since replacement, but unless other work was done, the crank, rod, bearings and valves still have 125.

GASGAS’s schedule calls for:
- **Minor engine service every 50 hours**, including piston replacement and cylinder, head and cam/rocker checks.
- **Major engine service every 100 hours**, including valves, connecting rod and its bearing, crank pin, engine bearings and lubrication-system work.
- Valve-clearance checks after the first hour, then **every 30 hours**.
- Oil/filter changes and screen cleaning after the first hour, then **every 10 hours and after every race**.

Those are scheduled service points—not predictions of when it will fail. Clean filtration and good oil care help, but easy starting and quiet running don’t prove the rod bearing is healthy. For motocross, I’d review the bottom-end service history and budget the major service rather than simply run toward 200.

Has the crank/rod or major engine service ever been done?

Also, the US drive-chain recall names the **2021 MC 450F**; have a GASGAS dealer confirm whether its free chain replacement was completed.

response.summary: A light, longstanding clutch-out chatter can be normal, particularly at idle in neutral. At 165 hours, changes in the noise or clutch operation matter more than the sound alone.
response.answer:
**Normal within limits:** if it’s a light chatter at idle in neutral, has always sounded the same, and the clutch works properly, it isn’t automatically a fault.

As general mechanical guidance, engine pulses can rattle the unloaded clutch and gearbox through their normal clearances. Pulling the clutch in disconnects the gearbox input from engine drive, so that chatter often quiets down. That lever response points toward the clutch/input side, but doesn’t prove everything is unworn.

You’re describing a **2017.5 450 SX-F**, while the selected Garage bike is a 2025; I wouldn’t apply its inspection limits to yours. At **165 hours**, worn basket damping, basket/hub notching or bearing wear deserve checking at the next clutch inspection, especially if its service history is unknown.

**Stop riding if it becomes a heavy knock or grinding, suddenly gets louder, or comes with slipping, creeping with the lever pulled in, difficult shifting or metal flakes in the oil/filter.**

**I’d budget for the top ends now rather than wait for compression to fall—especially the KX65 at nearly 60 hours.** Inspect and measure before deciding which parts need replacing.

The KX65 holding **170 psi**, and the KX85 holding **190 psi over nearly 40 hours**, are encouraging for ring sealing—provided you used the same gauge and test method. But compression cannot tell you whether the piston skirt is worn or developing a crack, or whether the small-end bearing needs attention. A piston can maintain compression and still fail mechanically.

As general small-bore two-stroke practice:
- **KX65:** inspect the top end now rather than extending its life solely on that reading.
- **KX85:** schedule an inspection too; if its piston hours before purchase are unknown, those 40 hours aren’t its total service time.

Have the piston, cylinder, rings, wrist pin and small-end bearing checked against Kawasaki’s limits. Hard racing makes replacement more urgent; gentle riding reduces wear but doesn’t make compression a replacement schedule.

The exact intervals and wear limits aren’t confirmed here without the model years; selecting each build gets the bike-specific figures. **Don’t run either with a new metallic rattle, knock or sudden power loss.**

question: I just picked up a 2023 and I'm just under 200 lbs, Vet B rider. ... I tried using the Racetech spring calculator but it's telling me to go softer on the forks ... What springs are you guys using that are near my size?

response.summary: For your roughly 200 lb weight and Vet B pace, fork springs at 5.1 N/mm are the sensible common-practice pick—not softer than stock.
response.answer:
I'd pick **fork springs at 5.1 N/mm** for your roughly 200 lb weight and Vet B pace. That's a tester-tested outdoor MX starting point for this generation, not Kawasaki's weight-chart recommendation.

Kawasaki's stock fork springs are **5.0 N/mm**, with **4.8 and 5.2 N/mm** factory options. Testers consistently report that this fork needs more braking support; several found slightly stiffer springs helped its balance without sacrificing corner-entry comfort.

- **5.1 N/mm fork springs:** my pick for your weight and pace, balancing hold-up and comfort.
- **5.2 N/mm fork springs:** worth considering if you're particularly aggressive, ride big jumps, or still dive and bottom with 5.1s—not my automatic choice just because you're near 200 lb.

Before accepting the calculator's softer result, double-check the exact model, riding category and whether it expects weight with or without gear. A calculator result isn't proof that this fork needs softening.

Confirm the choice on a familiar braking zone and landing: less dive, controlled travel use and no added small-bump deflection. If extra compression makes it harsh but doesn't provide support, look at valving rather than chasing clickers.

question: 2020 YZ 250 clutch springs. Been going through a clutch about every 20 hours. They always are adjusted right with play ... Used for mx and I am not a featherer. Should I change the springs out to a 450 F spring as I believe these are heavier.
message_sent: 2020 YZ 250 clutch springs. Been going through a clutch about every 20 hours. They always are adjusted right with play ... Used for mx and I am not a featherer. Should I change the springs out to a 450 F spring as I believe these are heavier.
rider_context: Motocross use; clutch lasts ~20 hours; free play kept adjusted; says he does not feather the clutch

response.summary: I would fit six fresh YZ250-spec springs, not unidentified YZ450F springs, and inspect the failed pack before buying heavier ones. Repeated 20-hour clutch replacements deserve a check of what is actually wearing or overheating.
response.answer:
**I’d use six fresh YZ250-spec springs—not swap in YZ450F springs blindly.** The 450 spring’s fit and installed clamping force aren’t confirmed here; heavier isn’t automatically compatible.

Since you’re maintaining free play and aren’t feathering it during MX, I wouldn’t blame lever adjustment or riding habits first. Weak springs can let the clutch slip under load without you touching the lever, generating heat and wearing the pack.

At the next pack inspection, use Yamaha’s figures:
- **Clutch springs:** 50 mm standard free length; 48 mm service limit. Replace as a set if short, damaged or uneven. Length alone doesn’t prove spring force is good.
- **Friction plates:** 2.90–3.10 mm standard; 2.80 mm wear limit. Measure each at four points.
- **Steel plates:** 0.20 mm maximum warpage; inspect for blue heat marks.

Also check basket/boss notching and that your transmission oil meets **SAE 10W-40, API SG or higher, JASO MA**. Notching mainly causes dragging or poor release; heat-marked plates point toward slipping.

**My pick: fresh OEM YZ250 springs first.** If a sound, correctly assembled pack still slips, use a heavier spring kit specifically listed for your 2020 YZ250; expect a harder lever pull. Don’t ride with active slipping.

When you replace it, is it slipping with burnt/thin plates, or dragging/grabbing with plates still within limits?

question: i just picked up a lightly used 22 tc 250, what are some of the worthwhile mods for these bikes? ... what aftermarket pipes work best? what jetting are people running? im really thinking of doing the 300 kit, any reason i shouldnt?
message_sent: i just picked up a lightly used 22 tc 250, what are some of the worthwhile mods for these bikes? ... what aftermarket pipes work best? what jetting are people running? im really thinking of doing the 300 kit, any reason i shouldnt?
rider_context: Lightly used bike; has a cone-valve/Trax suspension combo and linkage from his 350 to fit; considering a 300 big-bore kit

response.summary: Get the suspension and jetting sorted before adding displacement. My first exhaust pick is an FMF Factory Fatty; hold off on the 300 kit until you know whether you actually need more low-end torque.
response.answer:
I'd **sort the suspension and carb first, then try an FMF Factory Fatty before committing to a 300 kit**. A healthy 250 with clean jetting can feel much better without opening the engine.

### Worthwhile changes
- **Suspension for your weight and pace:** start with Husqvarna’s **105 mm riding sag and 35 mm static sag**. Correct fork air pressure and shock spring matter more than an exhaust if the bike isn’t balanced.
- **Tires matched to your dirt**, then gearing if a particular corner or straight calls for it. Stock gearing is **14/49**—don’t change it just because someone else does.
- Keep the stock airbox intact initially. One tester found venting sharpened throttle response, but slower riders didn’t necessarily prefer it, and jetting needs rechecking afterward.

### Pipes
**My all-around pick: FMF Factory Fatty**, listed for the 2020–2022 TC 250 generation. It’s the common choice when you want a broad motocross-style delivery rather than building everything around low-rpm riding.

For tight woods where low-end pull and pipe durability matter most, an **FMF Gnarly** is a common alternative; confirm its exact 2022 TC 250 application before buying. Neither pipe is a substitute for correct jetting, and a silencer alone wouldn’t be my first performance purchase.

### Jetting people run
Independent tests of this carbureted generation reported good results with **450 main, 35 pilot, 6BFY42-71 needle, third clip and air screw 1½ turns out**. That isn’t a universal setting—it also matches Husqvarna’s stock-engine chart for the following mild conditions:

| Temperature | Elevation | Main / pilot | Needle / clip | Air screw |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 61–75°F | 0–2,461 ft | 450 / 35 | 42-71 / third | 1½ out |
| 77–97°F | 0–2,461 ft | 440 / 32.5 | 42-71 / third | 1½ out |
| 99–120°F | 0–984 ft | 430 / 32.5 | 42-71 / third | 2 out |
| 99–120°F | 988–2,461 ft | 430 / 30 | 42-71 / third | 2 out |

These are stock engine/exhaust starting points, not instructions to lean your current setup blindly. Stop if it pings or detonates.

### The 300 kit
Worth considering for **low-end torque, taller-gear riding and less clutch work**. Reasons to wait: cost, potentially more tiring delivery, changed jetting requirements and race-class eligibility. Exact kit compatibility isn’t confirmed here; buy a matched conversion specified for the **2022 carbureted engine**, with the builder confirming head, piston and power-valve compatibility—not a cylinder alone.

Also verify the previous owner’s piston history: Husqvarna schedules replacement at **20 hours**, or **10 hours with regular sand use**. “Lightly used” isn’t a service record.

**Where do you ride—town/elevation, typical temperature, and mostly MX or trails?**

question: Looking to get as much extra power out of the 250 as possible without getting into engine work territory. Anyone have experience with both a 2024-2026 KX450, and '25/26 KX 250 with a Vortex, full PC exhaust, Airbox mod and possibly some gearing?
message_sent: Looking to get as much extra power out of the 250 as possible without getting into engine work territory. Anyone have experience with both a 2024-2026 KX450, and '25/26 KX 250 with a Vortex, full PC exhaust, Airbox mod and possibly some gearing?
rider_context: Currently on a KX450, considering downsizing to a 2025/2026 KX250; wants bolt-on power only (Vortex ECU, Pro Circuit exhaust, airbox mod, gearing)

response.summary: A mapped Vortex, full Pro Circuit exhaust and properly sealed intake kit are a sensible maximum bolt-on package for the 2025 KX250, but they will not give it KX450 torque. The strongest reported improvement is mid-to-top pull and recovery, not a huge bottom-end transformation.
response.answer:
**For maximum bolt-on power, I’d pick the Vortex mapped specifically for a full Pro Circuit Ti-6 and a properly sealed intake kit.** Confirm all three fit your ’25 before buying; the calibration needs to match the exhaust, intake and fuel you’ll actually run.

Here’s what the reported results support—not a back-to-back test of identical builds:

| | ’25/26 KX250 | ’24-on KX450 |
|---|---|---|
| Exhaust | Testers found stronger mid-to-top, smoother over-rev and better recovery; only a small low-end gain | A full Ti-6 dyno test went from 57.4 to 58.5 hp and 35.5 to 37.2 lb-ft, mainly midrange |
| ECU/intake package | Two owners report better response, but still slower-revving than the ’21–24 250 | One mapped Vortex/exhaust/open-airbox/race-fuel build gained almost 4 hp versus its stock ECU—not versus a completely stock bike |
| Stock gearing | 13/50 | 13/50 |

**The 250 package makes it easier to hold second and pull third; it doesn’t turn it into a 450.** There isn’t a confirmed measured horsepower gain for that complete 250 combination here.

For gearing, **if you’re still on 13/50, try 13/51**: several testers found better corner-exit pickup. It trades shorter gears and more shifting for stronger pull—it adds no engine horsepower.

My order: matched exhaust/intake/ECU package, then gearing. Use a purpose-built intake solution rather than cutting the airbox indiscriminately; keeping dirt out beats any small airflow gain.

question: I'm thinking about buying my son a new 22 Suzuki, it's brand new leftover ... I know the suspension is Stiff on this bike for somebody under 180 pounds, but he is 190 pounds. ... What exhaust recommendations do you make, and anything else would be helpful
message_sent: I'm thinking about buying my son a new 22 Suzuki, it's brand new leftover ... I know the suspension is Stiff on this bike for somebody under 180 pounds, but he is 190 pounds. ... What exhaust recommendations do you make, and anything else would be helpful
rider_context: Parent asking for adult son, 190 lb; son has ridden two-strokes since age 4 incl. lots of 125 experience, new to four-strokes

response.summary: At 190 lb, start with the stock suspension rather than automatically buying softer springs. My exhaust pick is a Yoshimura RS-12 full system, but suspension setup and proper leftover-bike preparation come first.
response.answer:
At **190 lb, I’d give the stock suspension a fair test before changing springs**. My exhaust pick is a **Yoshimura RS-12 full system**, a common choice for this bike—confirm the exact 2022 RM-Z250 application before buying.

- **Exhaust:** The Yoshimura is my pick for improving usable pull, not turning it into a class-leading horsepower bike. An FMF Factory 4.1 RCT system is another common choice, but I wouldn’t pay extra for titanium unless weight savings really matter. Neither system’s gains are confirmed here. Keep the stock exhaust initially if the budget is tight.
- **Fueling:** Suzuki specifies dual-injector EFI. Follow the exhaust maker’s fueling recommendations; budget for matching ECU tuning if required. Don’t assume an aggressive coupler automatically supplies the fueling a full system needs.
- **Suspension:** Testers consistently report stiff suspension, especially the fork, but his weight makes retaining the stock springs a sensible starting point. Commonly reported stock rates are **fork springs 5.0 N/mm and shock spring 52 N/mm**, not confirmed Suzuki-published figures. The commonly reported rider-sag baseline is **110 mm**; measure static sag alongside it before deciding on a shock spring. Don’t order softer springs just because lighter testers needed them.
- **Leftover preparation:** Make the deal include inspection of tire age/cracking, fork seals, linkage lubrication, cooling and brakes, plus fresh fuel and appropriate fluid service. Calendar age matters even with no riding hours.

**My spending order: proper dealer preparation, suspension setup, then the Yoshimura.**

question: I've always just run the stock stuff and never invested heavily into suspension outside of normal maintenance... but I'm wanting to now. My question is, where do I start and how much do I need to spend to make a noticeable difference?

response.summary: Start with spring fit and a proper setup session, not replacement suspension. Budget roughly $800–$1,400 for both ends serviced and revalved, allowing extra if springs are needed.
response.answer:
**Keep the stock fork and shock—start by matching the springs to you, then spend on valving if the setup still falls short.** Since you already do normal maintenance, another routine service alone isn’t the upgrade you’re looking for.

Here’s the spending order, with **general US shop budgeting estimates, not quotes for your KX250**:

1. **Setup session: roughly $100–$200.** Measure rider sag and free sag, check spring suitability, then test balance and clickers. This can make a noticeable difference if the current setup is off.
2. **Correct springs, if needed.** Kawasaki’s stock rates are **fork spring 5.0 N/mm** and **shock spring 54 N/mm**. Measure sag before choosing replacements; don’t pay for a revalve around springs that don’t suit you.
3. **Both ends serviced and revalved: roughly $800–$1,400; budget $1,000–$1,700 with springs.** Ask whether seals, bushings, springs and a follow-up tuning session are included. The goal is better bump comfort without giving away braking support or landing control.

**My pick: a local tuner who can watch you ride, retaining the stock units.** Skip expensive replacement cartridges or a shock initially. Get the tuner’s baseline sheet and confirm the improvement over the same rough section—not just by bouncing it in the garage.

question: I just bought a 250 sxf. I was told the bike has a lowering linkage ... My question is, do lowering linkages affect overall shock travel? I'm just wondering if it's worth having it swapped back to stock or leave it.
message_sent: I just bought a 250 sxf. I was told the bike has a lowering linkage ... My question is, do lowering linkages affect overall shock travel? I'm just wondering if it's worth having it swapped back to stock or leave it.
rider_context: Used bike with an aftermarket (Fasst-style) lowering linkage; has the stock linkage; previously rode a 450; year not stated

response.summary: A lowering linkage usually leaves the shock’s own stroke unchanged, but can change rear-wheel travel, progression and bottoming clearance. If you don’t need the lower seat height, I’d return it to stock.
response.answer:
**Usually it doesn’t shorten the shock’s stroke—but it can change how much the rear wheel moves through that stroke.** The linkage changes the leverage between the swingarm and shock, so it can also change spring feel, progression and bottoming resistance. Some kits retain nearly all the wheel travel; others reduce usable travel or require an internal travel limiter.

KTM lists **300 mm rear-wheel travel** for your stock 2025 250 SX-F. That isn’t the shock’s stroke, and it isn’t guaranteed with an unidentified lowering link.

**My pick: go back to stock if you’re comfortable with the standard seat height.** It restores a known suspension geometry and baseline. Keep the link if the lower height genuinely helps you, provided its maker confirms fitment, spring/sag requirements and full-compression clearance. A rear-only drop can also slow steering if the front hasn’t been balanced to match.

Your 2025 uses different linkage hardware from 2023–2024, so replacement parts must match the 2025 design. After returning to stock, KTM’s targets are **105 mm rider sag and 35 mm static sag**; don’t automatically apply those to the lowering kit.

What brand or markings are on the linkage?

question: Does a 13 tooth front sprocket wear out chains faster than a 14 tooth front sprocket?
message_sent: Does a 13 tooth front sprocket wear out chains faster than a 14 tooth front sprocket?

response.summary: Yes—a 13-tooth front sprocket generally wears a chain faster than a 14-tooth, all else equal, but maintenance and riding conditions often matter more.
response.answer:
**Yes, generally—a 13-tooth front is harder on the chain than a 14-tooth.** General drivetrain guidance: the smaller sprocket bends each chain joint farther as it wraps around, increasing articulation and wear. For the same torque at the countershaft, it also puts more tension into the chain.

It’s not automatically a big difference, and a 13-tooth is a perfectly usable choice. Dirt, lubrication, chain alignment and especially running the chain too tight can matter more.

If you’re choosing gearing and have clearance, **a 14-tooth front with a proportionally larger rear** gives similar gearing with gentler chain articulation. If the 13 gives you the gearing you need, run it—keep the slack correct and replace a hooked front sprocket rather than letting it chew up the chain.
